claim: Nothing holds the Moon up: no force pushes it away from Earth; gravity pulls it toward Earth all the time.
note: NASA's orbit page: an orbit is a fall around the planet. 'Nothing' = no supporting force.

claim: The Moon is constantly falling toward Earth: it falls about 1.36 mm below its straight-line path every second.
note: Excerpt: the Moon's deflection toward Earth is about 0.00136 m each second, enough to offset the straight-line path. Computed (c12): v²/(2r) for one second.

sentence: Look up tonight: it's about thirty Earths away.
claim: The Moon's mean distance (384,400 km) is about 30 Earth diameters (12,742 km).
note: Computed: 384,400 / 12,742 = 30.2 ('about thirty Earths'). 'Look up tonight': the Moon is visible most nights (and often by day).

sentence: And it moves sideways at about a kilometer every second.
claim: The Moon's mean orbital speed is 1.022 km/s.
note: Bible source. 'About a kilometer every second'; 'sideways' = along its orbit, at right angles to the pull.

sentence: That's New York to Boston in five minutes.
claim: New York City to Boston is about 306 km in a straight line: about 5 minutes at 1.022 km/s.
source_title: Distance from New York City to Boston (Geodatos)
note: Computed: 306 / 1.022 = 299 s = 5.0 min. The 346 km often quoted is the road distance.

sentence: The Moon would fly off in a straight line.
claim: With no net force acting, a moving object keeps moving at constant speed in a straight line (Newton's first law).
source_title: Newton's First Law of Motion (NASA Glenn Research Center)
note: Shown under 'thought experiment': gravity cannot be switched off.

sentence: Gravity bends it back toward us.
claim: Gravity pulls the Moon toward Earth, continuously bending its path away from the straight line into a closed orbit.
note: 'Into a circle': the Moon's orbit is nearly circular (eccentricity 0.055, Moon fact sheet).

sentence: Isaac Newton, the story goes, wondered if the pull that drops an apple reaches the Moon.
claim: Newton compared the fall of objects at Earth's surface with the Moon's motion to test whether one force (gravity, weakening with distance) explained both; the apple anecdote comes from later accounts (Stukeley; Conduitt).
source_title: Gravity and the Inverse Square Law (University of Cincinnati lecture notes)
note: The line says 'the story goes' for the apple: the anecdote is secondhand (told by Conduitt, who had it from his wife; and by Stukeley). The comparison itself (the 'Moon test') is Newton's. No date is spoken (the 1666 date is not confirmed by a primary source here).

sentence: The Moon is sixty times farther from Earth's center than the apple.
claim: The Moon is about 60 Earth radii (6,371 km) from Earth's centre; an apple at the surface is 1 Earth radius from it.
note: Computed: 384,400 / 6,371 = 60.3. An apple at the surface is one Earth radius from the centre.

sentence: So the pull there is thirty-six hundred times weaker.
claim: Gravity weakens with the square of distance, so at 60 times the distance from Earth's centre it is 60² = 3,600 times weaker.
source_title: Gravity and the Inverse Square Law (University of Cincinnati lecture notes)
note: Excerpt: the Moon's pull is weaker by a factor of 60² = 3600; its acceleration about 0.00272 m/s², precisely the observed acceleration of the Moon in its orbit.

sentence: Then in one minute, the Moon should fall as far as an apple falls in one second.
claim: At 1/3,600 of an apple's acceleration, the Moon falls in 60 seconds as far as an apple falls in 1 second (60² = 3,600): Newton's own comparison (Principia, Book III, Proposition 4).
source_title: Gravity and the Inverse Square Law (University of Cincinnati lecture notes)
note: Computed: ½ × (9.8/3600) × 60² = 4.9 m = ½ × 9.8 × 1². The Principia framing (Book III, Prop. 4, 'in one minute … about 15 Paris feet') is from the independent reviewer's note, not a search excerpt; an astronomer should confirm the citation.

claim: Dropped from rest, an object at Earth's surface falls about 4.9 m in the first second; the Moon falls about 4.9 m below its straight line in one minute.
note: Excerpt: an apple falls 4.9 meters in 1 second; in one second the Moon falls 0.00136 m. Computed: 0.00136 m × 60² = 4.9 m. 'About five meters'.

claim: The Moon's observed fall (from its 1.022 km/s speed on a 384,400 km orbit, v²/r = 0.00272 m/s²) matches the 1/3,600 prediction to about 1%: 1.36 mm in one second, 4.9 m in one minute.
note: Computed: (1022 m/s)² / 3.844e8 m = 0.002717 m/s²; 9.81 / 3,600 = 0.002725 (with 60.3 radii: 0.002697). 'And it does' = almost exactly. Relative to Earth: the Sun accelerates Earth and the Moon almost equally, so it drops out. Newton's own figure: 'a little less than the twentieth of an inch' a second (All the Year Round, via djo.org.uk).

sentence: So the pull that drops an apple is the very same pull that holds the Moon.
claim: The same gravity that makes objects fall at Earth's surface holds the Moon in its orbit (Newton's universal gravitation).
source_title: Gravity and the Inverse Square Law (University of Cincinnati lecture notes)

sentence: Light time, Earth to Moon: one point three seconds.
claim: Light crosses the Moon's mean distance (384,400 km) in about 1.28 seconds.
note: Computed: 384,400 / 299,792 = 1.282 s ('one point three seconds'; 1.21–1.35 s over the month).

sentence: You always see the Moon that late.
claim: Moonlight takes about 1.3 seconds to reach Earth, so you always see the Moon as it was about 1.3 seconds earlier.
source_title: What Is a Light-Year? (NASA Space Place)
note: The reflected sunlight left the Sun about 8 min 20 s before that; the Moon's image is 1.3 s old.

sentence: Every moment, all the way round.
claim: Gravity pulls the Moon toward Earth at every moment, at right angles to its motion, continuously bending its straight-line path into a closed orbit.
note: Same as c6: the pull acts continuously.

sentence: The heavens, people believed, had their own rules.
claim: In Aristotle's physics, followed for centuries, the heavens beyond the Moon were made of a different element (aether) moving naturally in circles, with different rules from falling bodies on Earth; Newton's universal gravitation united the two.
source_title: From Aristotle to Early Modern Science (Jan Garrett, Western Kentucky University)
note: Excerpts: above the sphere of the Moon there was no change except circular movement; the aether moved in a circle about the centre of the cosmos. Rochester (ast104) and NYU lecture notes describe the 'Newtonian synthesis' uniting the terrestrial and celestial realms.
